content: Developers building multi-agent systems need an expanded agentMom framework that provides reusable communication capabilities for agents and their conversations. Agents should be able to communicate with one recipient, selected groups, or all agents on a local network, join and leave communication groups, and choose whether messages require protection. The new framework must remain usable with applications based on the existing agentMom environment.

Right now, teams building agent-based applications have to solve communication in a lot of different ways, which creates inconsistency and slows development. The opportunity is to give them a reusable framework so agents can talk reliably within a local network, coordinate in groups, and manage protected messages without each project reinventing that plumbing.
Success would mean developers can plug this into existing agentMom-based applications and immediately use it for normal day-to-day agent coordination with less custom code. In practice, agents should be able to connect, join or leave groups, send to a specific agent or a broader audience, and do it predictably with the right level of message protection when needed.

It will typically be built by the platform or framework development team, the people maintaining agentMom itself. For a specific application, the application developers or solution engineers would usually configure which agents can communicate, what groups exist, and whether protection is enabled for certain message flows. Day to day, the main users would be the agents inside those applications, while the human developers would mostly interact with it when setting up or troubleshooting the communication behavior.

In everyday use, a recipient just means one specific agent or endpoint that a message is meant for. A selected group means a defined set of agents that have been organized for a shared purpose, and all agents means a broadcast to everyone available on the local network who can receive it. Protected messages would mean messages that need some extra handling so the contents aren’t exposed or altered in transit.

At minimum, I’d expect a message to carry who sent it, who it is for, the actual content, and some kind of message type or purpose so the receiver knows how to handle it. It should also have a timestamp and an identifier so it can be tracked, deduplicated, or correlated with a response if needed. If protection is involved, there should be something in the structure that indicates that status and whatever metadata is needed to process it correctly.

People would expect it to be fast enough that agents can coordinate in near real time for ordinary workflow tasks, without noticeable delays becoming a bottleneck. Delivery should be dependable within the local network, and if something can’t be delivered, the framework should make that visible rather than failing silently. For protected messages, the extra handling should not slow everything down too much in normal use.

A conversation would usually start when one agent initiates a message to another agent or to a group, and then continues as a back-and-forth until the task is complete. Group membership would change when an agent joins a group to participate in a shared activity or leaves when it no longer needs those messages. End of a conversation is usually just when the exchange is finished, while group membership ending means the agent stops receiving that group’s traffic.

Existing agentMom applications should keep running without major rewrites, ideally with their current communication flows still behaving the same unless a developer chooses to use the new features. The basic single-recipient messaging and any established workflows around agent interaction need to remain compatible so teams are not forced to rework working systems. In practice, the new framework should feel like an extension of what is already there, not a replacement that breaks existing behavior.

It should be built so new communication patterns can be added in a modular way, without changing the core behavior every time a new use case comes up. I’d expect developers to be able to plug in new message handling or routing logic while still using the same basic agentMom conventions for sending, receiving, and group management. The key is that extensions should fit naturally into the existing workflow instead of creating a parallel system that feels disconnected.

Yes, I’d want a safe default rather than guessing. If a message type or delivery path is not recognized, the framework should either route it through the most conservative supported path or reject it clearly with an explanation, especially if protection is involved. For anything protected, it should never downgrade security automatically just to make delivery happen.

It needs to work within a local network setup and stay lightweight enough that agents can run without heavy infrastructure or manual administration. I’d also expect it to tolerate mixed environments where some applications are older agentMom-based systems and others use the expanded framework, so compatibility is important. Beyond that, I don’t know of any very specific hard limits yet, but it should avoid introducing a lot of operational overhead.

It should support a kind of drop-in deployment where the old applications can connect using their current setup and don’t need special migration steps just to keep working. Configuration should stay simple and preferably default to the existing behavior unless someone explicitly turns on the new communication features. Operationally, I’d want the framework to isolate the newer capabilities so older applications aren’t forced to understand them or be configured for them.

I’d prefer it not to depend on any external cloud service for the core communication path, because that would make the drop-in behavior harder for existing applications. It should work locally within the agentMom environment and use whatever endpoints or discovery mechanisms are already available there, rather than requiring new mandatory infrastructure. If there are optional services for advanced features, those should stay optional and not be required for older applications to function.

I’d expect a typical deployment to be in the tens of agents, with maybe a handful of groups active at once, not hundreds or thousands. If it can scale beyond that, that’s great, but the day-to-day expectation is a fairly small local network of cooperating agents. The important thing is that common use stays responsive and simple to manage.

It should fail closed for protected messages if it can’t confirm a valid delivery path. I wouldn’t want it to silently reroute protected content through an unverified fallback, and I’d prefer it surface a clear delivery error quickly so the sender knows the message did not go through. If there’s a retry, it should only be against another path that is equally trusted and explicitly supported.

At minimum, I’d expect a sender, a recipient, and some kind of message identifier to be mandatory for one-to-one communication. If the message is protected, then the protection-related fields should also be required so the receiver knows how to handle it correctly. A response correlation field should be optional in general, but necessary whenever the sender expects a reply or needs to match the response back to the original message.

Only agents that are part of the intended group or visible on the local network should be eligible to receive it, and the framework should respect whatever membership and authorization rules are in place for that context. I’d also expect protected messages to be restricted more tightly, so even if an agent is technically in the group, it should be excluded if it hasn’t been cleared to handle that message type or protection level. In practice, yes, there can be exclusions for agents that are offline, not fully joined, or not authorized for the specific communication.

The framework should deliver to the members that are currently valid and available, and treat the others as non-deliverable rather than blocking the whole group exchange. If a member has left or no longer meets membership rules, it should simply be excluded from that message flow. If someone is only temporarily unavailable, I’d expect a normal delivery failure or retry behavior, but not a hard stop for everyone else in the group.

I’d expect a short retry window with a bounded number of attempts, enough to catch brief network or agent hiccups but not long enough to stall the conversation. After that, it should mark the delivery as failed and notify the sender, and probably log it for traceability. I don’t have a precise timing in mind yet, so that would need to be set based on the expected local network behavior.

Yes, there may be some organizational restrictions, especially around protected messages and audit logs, but I don’t have a finalized policy document to point to yet. My expectation is that the framework should minimize retention by default and avoid logging message contents unless explicitly allowed. For anything more specific, we’d need to confirm with the team that owns the deployment policies.

For a protected one-to-one message, I’d expect the protection type or mode, plus whatever key, reference, or token is needed for the receiver to unwrap or validate it. If there’s any integrity or authenticity metadata like a signature or checksum, that should be included as well. I’m not sure yet whether we need a separate policy label in the envelope or whether that belongs in the payload.

A retry on an alternative path should only be allowed if the protection requirements can still be preserved end to end, so the message wouldn’t be exposed or altered in transit. If the alternative path would weaken encryption, break validation, or violate the sender’s chosen protection level, then it should fail immediately. In other words, reroute is fine for transport problems, but not if the protection itself would be compromised.

The main factor should be who needs to act on the label. If intermediaries need it for routing, filtering, or enforcement, it has to stay in the envelope in a visible form; if only the receiver needs it, it can be embedded in the protected payload. I’d also expect some cases where policy must be visible to network controls even though the content stays hidden, but I don’t know the exact rule split yet.

For near-real-time coordination, I’d expect the framework to treat delays of more than a few seconds as problematic, especially when agents are waiting on each other to continue a workflow. Slower behavior may be acceptable for background tasks, bulk group broadcasts, or anything that is explicitly not time-sensitive. I don’t have a hard threshold yet, so that would need to be agreed based on the target use cases.

In most cases it should fail and notify the sender once the retry window is exhausted, so the sender can decide what to do next. I could see a special exception for low-priority or non-urgent messages where the system is configured to keep them queued a bit longer, but that should be explicit rather than automatic. For anything workflow-critical, I’d lean toward a clear failure instead of indefinite waiting.

That should be driven by message priority, sender policy, and maybe the recipient group’s own retention rules if those exist. I’d expect there to be a firm maximum so the queue doesn’t grow without bound, but I don’t know the exact duration yet. My guess is it should be short and configurable, with a clear cutoff rather than open-ended holding.

Yes, I think some of the more advanced routing and policy behaviors could be deferred for the first release, especially anything that depends on complex network-wide discovery or automatic optimization. The first version should focus on reliable one-to-one, group, and broadcast communication with basic protection choices and compatibility with existing agentMom applications. Anything beyond that, like smarter rerouting or richer policy negotiation, could come later if the core framework is stable.

The first release should be tolerant of older applications that only use a subset of the expected behavior, as long as the core message can still be understood and delivered safely. If an endpoint is missing optional fields or older conventions, the framework should degrade gracefully and not break the whole exchange. But if the message format is too incomplete to interpret reliably, then it should fail clearly rather than guess.

For the first release, basic routing and policy rules should be applied whenever the destination is clear and the framework can deliver the message without extra interpretation. If a message can go on the default path, I’d prefer the system to do that rather than attempt any smarter rerouting or negotiation, since that keeps behavior predictable and compatible with the existing environment. Only if the default path clearly can’t satisfy the required protection or delivery constraints should it stop and report the issue.

For protected messages, I’d expect content to be minimized in logs by default, so ideally the framework should not retain the actual message body unless there’s an explicit operational need and the sender policy allows it. Basic metadata and delivery traces can probably be kept for troubleshooting and audit, but anything sensitive should be redacted or tokenized where possible. If the message is marked highly sensitive or the sender requests stricter protection, then even some metadata may need to be suppressed, though I’d want the exact retention rules confirmed with the security side.

That should only be allowed when the sender has opted into that behavior and the message policy explicitly permits it. Even then, I’d expect hard limits around security level, recipient scope, and message criticality, so the framework can’t silently change the path in ways that weaken protection or delivery guarantees. If those conditions aren’t met, it should leave the message on the default path and report that no alternate handling was applied.

In that case, it should not reroute it at all. The framework should keep the message on the normal delivery path, or reject the alternate handling request if even the default path would violate the policy constraints. It should also make it clear that the reason was safety or policy restriction, not a technical routing failure.
